newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark's premier apologises over Rushdie row.
newsitem.headline: Denmark's premier apologises over Rushdie row.

text.p: Denmark on Sunday apologised for mishandling a planned visit by British author Salman Rushdie which it initially banned on security grounds and then rescheduled after a storm of domestic and foreign protest.

Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen told a news conference that the government's initial decision, taken out of fear that it could not adequately protect Rushdie from Islamic zealots, was correct but the way in which it was communicated to Rushdie was deficient and unsatisfactory.
"The government gives Rushdie our unconditional apology," Rasmussen said.

Indian-born Rushdie has lived in hiding and with permanent protection since 1989 when Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa, death sentence, against him for his novel "The Satanic Verses", saying it blasphemed against Islam.

He was recently invited to Copenhagen to receive a European Union literary award but last Thursday was told that publicity for the presentation, and police resources stretched by a Nordic biker gang war, made it impossible to guarantee his safety.
The decision brought howls of outrage from fellow authors in Denmark, Sweden and Britain and Danish members of parliament threatened a vote of no confidence in the minority government.
On Friday Danish Culture Minister Jytte Hilten appeared to patch things up with Rushdie, inviting him to come to Copenhagen to accept the award at some time before the New Year.
Rushdie welcomed the news but Danish newspapers continued to lambast Rasmussen, Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen and Justice Minister Bjoern Westh.

A front-page cartoon in Saturday's Berlingske Tidende showed the three men each studiously shooting himself in the foot and there have been calls for Westh's dismissal, although some papers report that Rasmussen approved the Rushdie ban.
Presentation of awards to Rushdie, Austrian writer Christoph Ransmayer and Danish author and translator Thorkild Bjoernvig was originally to have made on November 14 in Copenhagen.
It is this year's European Cultural Capital, a title which rotates around the EU.
In the past two years Rushdie has travelled widely abroad and in Britain, giving lectures and attending literary events.
Iran says it is powerless to lift the fatwa, which can only be revoked by the man who issued it. But Khomeini died in 1989.
Rushdie, born to Moslem parents in Bombay, has always rejected Iran's charge of blasphemy.
